name: OxfordVR gameChange
one_liner: Automated VR therapy for severe agoraphobic avoidance in psychosis, offered by some NHS mental health teams in England. Not available in the US.
best_for: Adults and young people (16+) with psychosis in England who rarely leave home because of anxiety
NHS mental health teams looking for VR-guided exposure therapy their patients can use with staff support
not_for: People in the US or outside the NHS: it is not sold to the public and has no FDA clearance
Anyone in crisis: call or text 988 (US) or 111 option 2 / 999 (UK)
People with agoraphobia or anxiety who do not have psychosis
short_description: VR therapy where a virtual coach guides you through everyday situations, used by some NHS teams for agoraphobic avoidance in psychosis.
long_description: gameChange is an automated virtual reality therapy developed by the University of Oxford, OxfordVR and NHS trusts. Wearing a VR headset, you practise everyday situations such as a café, a shop or a bus while a virtual coach guides you through cognitive therapy techniques, with a mental health worker present. In a 2022 trial in England of 346 people with psychosis, adding gameChange to usual care reduced agoraphobic avoidance and distress at 6 weeks compared with usual care alone; the overall effect was small, and the largest benefit was in people with the most severe avoidance. In 2023 NICE's early value assessment said it can be used in the NHS for people 16 and over with psychosis and severe agoraphobic avoidance while more evidence is gathered, and a real-world trial is running from 2025 to 2027. It is offered only through some NHS services; it is not sold to individuals, and in the US it has an FDA Breakthrough Device designation (2022) but no clearance. OxfordVR merged with US company BehaVR in 2022, and a 2025 study says XR Health now holds the commercial licence.
patient_summary: gameChange is VR therapy where a virtual coach helps you practise going into places like shops and buses that you have been avoiding. It is for people with psychosis and is offered only through some NHS mental health teams in England, with a staff member supporting you. You can't buy it yourself, and it isn't available in the US.

pricing.starting_price: Through NHS services only; organisations contact the vendor
pricing.notes: No self-pay option. Free to patients where an NHS mental health team offers it; NHS organisations license it from the vendor. No published price.

privacy.notes: Delivered by NHS teams, so your records are handled under the NHS trust's UK data protection rules. We could not read a product privacy policy; HIPAA does not apply in the UK.

seo.title: OxfordVR gameChange: NHS VR Therapy for Agoraphobia
seo.meta_description: gameChange is the first NHS-approved VR therapy for severe agoraphobia in psychosis patients. Automated CBT with virtual coach from Oxford University research.

faqs.a: gameChange is an automated VR cognitive therapy program for treating severe agoraphobia in patients with psychosis. It's the first VR treatment approved for NHS mental health services.
Patients use VR to safely practice re-entering everyday situations with guidance from a virtual coach. The automated CBT-based therapy doesn't require a real therapist during sessions.
gameChange was developed by Oxford University, Oxford VR, Oxford Health NHS Foundation Trust, and nine NHS Trusts, led by Professor Daniel Freeman's 20+ years of clinical VR research.
gameChange treats adults with severe agoraphobia who have psychotic disorders. It's particularly effective for patients who are largely housebound and have the most severe symptoms.

clinical_trials.study: gameChange VR therapy plus usual care vs usual care alone in patients with psychosis in England

citation.authors: Freeman D, Lambe S, Kabir T, et al.
citation.title: Automated virtual reality therapy to treat agoraphobic avoidance and distress in patients with psychosis (gameChange): a multicentre, parallel-group, single-blind, randomised, controlled trial in England with mediation and moderation analyses

clinical_trials.outcome: Reduced agoraphobic avoidance and distress at 6 weeks vs usual care (small effect, d -0.18 for avoidance); largest benefit in people with severe avoidance. No difference in serious adverse events.
clinical_trials.study_design: Multicentre single-blind randomised controlled trial (usual care control)

primary_uses: Practising everyday situations you avoid, in VR
Guided exposure with a virtual coach
Reducing anxiety about leaving home in psychosis
Use alongside NHS mental health care

availability.note: Only through some NHS mental health services in England (NICE early value assessment, 2023). Not sold to individuals and not available in the US (FDA Breakthrough designation only).
